title: Habit Building
summary: Pick a cue → Start small → Count fairly → Return after a miss
subtitle: Make a useful action easier to return to when life gets busy.

blocks.text: A fitness app may announce a fresh start before you’ve found both socks. A useful routine needs a starting point that fits your day. Practise one small action, and don’t judge yourself for a missed chance.
Make healthy actions feel automatic, one small step at a time.
blocks.detail: A clear cue and a small first step cut down the decisions you face when your day is already full.
blocks.extra: Section 03 shows how to build a routine you can repeat.

sections.title: Give the action a starting point

blocks.text: Grabbing your keys on the way out takes little thought. A familiar event can become linked with what you do next. That event is a cue, and the learned response to it is a habit.
A plan is a good start, but it doesn’t mean an action is already a habit. Repeating a small action after a steady cue gives your brain the chance to learn the link.

This lesson teaches everyday planning, not treatment. For a new movement routine, use CSEP’s Get Active Questionnaire and follow its advice about getting more help. Choose an action that fits your abilities and any care advice you already have.

sections.title: Build a routine you can repeat

blocks.text: Choose one action with a benefit you care about. “Move more” leaves the next step open. “Walk indoors for three comfortable minutes after lunch on workdays” tells you what to try. A short action can be a starting point without covering all your activity needs.

Choose a cue that already happens on the days you plan to practise. Finishing lunch may be more reliable than a clock time when your shifts move around. Check that the cue leaves you free to act. Serving someone else lunch may not.
Test the cue before adding reminders. For two days, notice whether the event happens and whether you have room to act afterward. A cue you rarely meet needs changing.

Write an if/then line: “If I put my lunch dish in the sink on a workday, then I’ll walk the clear hallway for three minutes.” An easier version might be one comfortable minute. Decide ahead of time that either version counts, and write down which one you did.

Set up your space so the first step is easy to find. Keep safe shoes where you’ll see them, while keeping exits and walkways clear. If the real barrier is that nobody can cover your care duties, equipment won’t solve it. You may need a support arrangement.
Keep tracking simple: mark full version, easier version or missed. The record should help you choose your next step. It doesn’t need a mood rating or a public streak.

items.title: “After 21 or 30 days, every action becomes automatic.”
items.text: Habit research finds big differences between people and actions. In one well-known study, it took a median of 66 days for a new action to feel automatic, with a range from 18 to 254 days. No calendar deadline can promise a routine will happen without thought.

blocks.text: When you miss a chance, return at the next planned cue. If misses keep happening, ask whether the cue, the size of the action or your support needs changing. You can revise a plan without erasing the practice you’ve already done.

sections.title: Fictional learning story: Theo’s tea tin

blocks.text: Theo’s tea tin
paragraphs: Theo was a home caregiver in Halifax who also helped his father at home. He wanted a movement break before his evening tasks. His walking shoes sat beside the tea tin, but he usually went straight from the kettle to the laundry.

One Thursday, he found an old note that said, “Walk at five.” That week, not one shift had ended at five. His plan depended on a time his work couldn’t protect, and the blank boxes on his calendar made him want to quit.

He thought about adding more alarms. Instead, he chose a new starting point. After putting his work bag by the tea tin, he would walk indoors for three minutes, once his father was settled. His easier version was one minute. He planned four chances that week.

On Monday and Tuesday he did the full version. Wednesday’s late visit left room for only the easier one. He marked each day honestly, not as three matching ticks, and left Thursday blank when an urgent task took the whole evening.

On Friday, his father moved the tea tin to a high shelf to clear the counter. Theo set down his work bag and still remembered the walk. The real cue had been putting down the bag, not seeing the tin. He stuck a small reminder where the bag always went.

At his review, Theo counted three of four planned chances done, including one easier version. He kept the same amount for another week and asked his sister to cover one evening task. The tea tin came back to the counter, but his plan no longer depended on where anyone kept the tea.

blocks.text: Theo changed a cue that didn’t fit his shifts. His plan worked, even though it still took some thought.
Keep a way back, and a busy day never ends the habit.
blocks.detail: An easier version and an honest review help you return after a crowded day, without starting the whole plan over.
blocks.extra: Section 05 gives you a one-week plan to try.

blocks.text: Use this example to test your setup, not to prove your fitness. Choose a comfortable indoor route or a familiar seated move that suits you. Keep any movement within your abilities. These amounts are examples, not a personal medical prescription.
Adjustable one-week example

items.title: Cue: put the lunch dish in the sink on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Friday.
Full version: one minute easing into a walk, two minutes at a comfortable pace, and one minute slowing down. Total: four minutes.
Easier version: one minute of comfortable movement, starting and ending gently.
Setup: clear the route before the week begins and put a four-box tracker near the cue.
Review: take five minutes on Sunday to count chances and choose one change, if needed.

blocks.text: In this example, Monday and Thursday are full versions, Tuesday is the easier version and Friday is missed. That’s three of four planned chances, with nine minutes of movement in total: four plus one plus four. Wednesday and the weekend weren’t planned, so they aren’t missed chances.
Write down your planned days before the week starts. Keep the original count visible if life changes, and note what changed. That keeps your review honest without quietly dropping the hard days.

For the next week, repeat the same level if it still takes effort. If you choose to increase, change one thing, like adding one comfortable minute to the full version on the same days. There’s no deadline to increase, and a shorter plan may suit you better.
Check your indoor backup before bad weather arrives. A building hallway must be clear and open to you. A small room or a seated option may be more practical.

items.title: “Missing Friday means I should double Monday’s activity.”
items.text: Go back to the planned amount. Extra work isn’t a penalty you owe for a missed chance.

blocks.text: Stop for pain, feeling faint, chest symptoms or extreme breathlessness, and get urgent help for possible heart attack symptoms. Choose safe conditions for the season. In winter, use the indoor route instead of an icy entrance.
Insider tip: Put one review question beside your tracker: “What made starting hard?” Answer it before you buy a new tool. A smaller action or better support may fix the real barrier.
Quick Check

items.title: Is a written plan proof that a habit is established?
items.text: A plan guides practice; a habit is a learned response to a cue.

items.title: Can a pre-planned easier version count as practice?
items.text: Record which version you used so the review stays honest.

items.title: You planned four chances and completed three. Do two unplanned rest days count as misses?
items.text: Report three out of four, and leave unplanned days out of the count.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: Your shifts change, but you always put away your lunch dish. Which cue best fits? A. Exactly noon. · B. Putting away the dish when time is available. · C. Whenever you feel motivated.
items.text: An event in your routine can fit changing shifts better than a fixed clock time. It also needs a safe chance to act.

items.title: You planned five chances, used the full version twice and the easier version twice, and missed once. How do you report it? A. Four of five, naming both versions. · B. Two of five. · C. Five of five because you meant to act.
items.text: Both agreed versions count. Naming them shows what happened.

items.title: You still need a reminder after 30 days. What is a useful next step? A. Assume you failed. · B. Remove all reminders. · C. Review the cue and keep practising a manageable action.
items.text: A fixed number of days does not prove automaticity. Reminders can still help.

items.title: Write an if/then plan with an easier version and a return step after a miss.
items.text: If I finish lunch on Monday or Thursday, I will walk indoors for three comfortable minutes, or one minute on a busy day. After a miss, I will return at the next planned cue.

blocks.text: Link one small action to a reliable cue. Prepare an easier version, count planned chances honestly, and return at the next chance after a miss.
Write your one-week plan using these questions. Name the days before you begin, and keep private health details out.
Include an if/then sentence, a review date and a way back after a missed chance. At your review, keeping the same amount is a fine choice.

items.title: Cue
items.text: An event or setting that can prompt an action.

items.title: Habit
items.text: A learned response linked to a familiar cue.

items.title: Automaticity
items.text: Doing an action with little conscious thought.

items.title: Easier version
items.text: A smaller action agreed on before a difficult day.

items.title: Planned opportunity
items.text: A chance you chose in advance to practise.

How will you return after a missed chance?
samples: Name something you already do, such as putting your lunch dish in the sink.
For example: three minutes of walking, or one minute on a busy day.
For example: If I put my work bag down, then I’ll walk the hallway for three minutes.
For example: Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday.
Clear a space, arrange help, set a simple reminder, or not sure.
For example: I’ll start again at the next planned cue, with no extra minutes.
